Relationships: 'Ich verstehe mich gut mit...' (I get on well with...), 'Wir streiten uns' (We argue).

Nominative (subject), accusative (object), dative (indirect object), genitive (possession). Endings change accordingly.

du = informal singular (family, friends); Sie = formal (always capitalised), used with strangers, teachers.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Area A: Everyday Activities — a core area of GCSE German.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area A: Everyday Activities brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area A: Everyday Activities.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I get on well with my mother'?
options: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meiner Mutter.
Ich verstehe mich gut mit meine Mutter.
Ich verstehe mir gut mit meiner Mutter.
Ich verstehen mich gut mit meine Mutter.

mcqs.q: Which form of 'you' do you use addressing a German teacher?
options: Sie
du
ihr
es

mcqs.q: How do you say 'I drove to Munich' in the perfect tense?
options: Ich habe nach München gefahren.
Only the first word of a sentence.
Ich fahre nach München.
Ich bin nach München gefahren.

mcqs.q: Which words are capitalised in German?
options: Only the first word of a sentence.
Only proper nouns, as in English.
All nouns (and the first word of a sentence).
Ich fahre nach München.

mcqs.q: When describing a past holiday in writing, which past tense is more common in German?
options: Perfect tense (ich bin gefahren) for most verbs, but PRETERITE for sein, haben, modal verbs (war, hatte, konnte).
Always use present tense and add a time word.
Always use the preterite like English simple past.
Only the first word of a sentence.
